title: Hidden Thread
description: Five source-backed questions share one precise connection. Find it after the fifth reveal.

threads.title: The names inside the facts
threads.teaser: Five answers. One human trail hiding in their names.
choices: They all hide the name of a real person
They were all coined for radio broadcasts
They all began as legal terms
They were all invented in the same decade
threads.connection: Every trail leads to a person whose name became part of an object, word, test, or fictional identity.

links.explanation: The saxophone carries inventor Adolphe Sax’s surname.
To boycott grew from the organized isolation of land agent Charles Boycott.
A silhouette preserves the surname of French finance minister Étienne de Silhouette.
The T in CAPTCHA invokes Alan Turing and the Turing test.
Ian Fleming borrowed James Bond from the author of a Caribbean bird guide.

threads.title: A message finds a medium
threads.teaser: The questions jump across centuries, but each leaves information somewhere it can travel or survive.
choices: They all concern lost musical instruments
They all use a medium to transmit or preserve information
They all originated in university laboratories
They all depend on satellite navigation
threads.connection: Each fact turns on a medium that carries information: electrical images, a phonograph record, a website, a clay tablet, or newspapers.

links.explanation: Alexander Bain’s image-transmission work became part of the fax’s technical ancestry.
Voyager carries sounds and greetings on a physical phonograph record.
The first website explained the World Wide Web through the Web itself.
A cuneiform tablet preserved rules that helped scholars reconstruct an ancient game.
Newspaper images carried news of Guernica’s bombing to Picasso.

threads.title: Unexpected job descriptions
threads.teaser: A stone, syrup, cloth, plastic bubbles, and a pencil core are moonlighting.
choices: They were all first used underwater
Ordinary materials are doing a surprising job
They were all patented by film studios
threads.connection: Every answer reveals a familiar material or object used in a role most people would not guess from looking at it.

links.explanation: A sea otter keeps a stone as a reusable shell-opening tool.
Chocolate syrup played convincing blood in a black-and-white film.
A suspended muslin funnel became a miniature tornado.
Air-bubble sheets were first pitched as textured wallpaper before becoming packaging.
A pencil’s so-called lead is chiefly graphite mixed with clay.

threads.title: Nothing is quite standing still
threads.teaser: The movement can take seconds, hours, years, or geological ages—but it is always there.
choices: Every answer depends on hidden or slow movement
Every answer happens only at high altitude
Every answer was discovered by astronauts
Every answer changes exactly once per year
threads.connection: Things that look fixed—continents, a day’s length, a tower, the body in microgravity, even airflow through the nose—are changing or cycling.

links.explanation: A tectonic plate creeps at a rate comparable to fingernail growth.
The Moon’s tidal influence very gradually lengthens Earth’s day.
Uneven solar heating makes the Eiffel Tower expand and lean slightly.
Microgravity lets an astronaut’s spine lengthen temporarily.
Tissue swelling alternates between nostrils in the nasal cycle.
